definitions.text: A particle which expresses the relation of connection or addition. It is used to conjoin a word with a word, a clause with a clause, or a sentence with a sentence. women," that is, two very different sorts of women. (b) By a rhetorical figure, notions, one of which is modificatory of the other, are connected by and; as, "the tediousness and process of my travel," that is, the tedious process, etc.; "thy fair and outward character," that is, thy outwardly fair character, Schmidt's Shak. Lex.
In order to; -- used instead of the infinitival to, especially after try, come, go. At least to try and teach the erring soul. Milton.
It is sometimes, in old songs, a mere expletive. When that I was and a little tiny boy. Shak.

If; though. See An, conj. [Obs.] Chaucer. As they will set an house on fire, and it were but to roast their eggs. Bacon. And so forth, and others; and the rest; and similar things; and other things or ingredients. The abbreviation, etc. (et cetera), or &c., is usually read and so forth.
Doubt; uncertainty. [Obs.] Shelford.
A silicate of aluminium, occurring usually in thick rhombic prisms, nearly square, of a grayish or pale reddish tint. It was first discovered in Andalusia, Spain.
Moving moderately slow, but distinct and flowing; quicker than larghetto, and slower than allegretto.
A movement or piece in andante time.
Rather quicker than andante; between that allegretto. andantino as its diminutive, or "less going," define the latter as slower than andante.
Red orpiment. Coxe.
Pertaining to the Andes.
A kind of triclinic feldspar found in the Andes.
An eruptive rock allied to trachyte, consisting essentially of a triclinic feldspar, with pyroxene, hornblende, or hypersthene.
Andean; as, Andine flora.
A utensil for supporting wood when burning in a fireplace, one being placed on each side; a firedog; as, a pair of andirons.
The dissection of a human body, especially of a male; androtomy. Coxe.
Having a human head (upon an animal's body), as the Egyptian sphinx.
Having perfect and staminate flowers on different plants. -- An`dro*di*o"cism, -di*e"cism (#), n.

Uniting both sexes in one, or having the characteristics of both; being in nature both male and female; hermaphroditic. Owen. The truth is, a great mind must be androgynous. Coleridge.

A meteor appearing to radiate from a point in the constellation Andromeda, -- whence the name. A shower of these meteors takes place every year on November 27th or 28th. The Andromedes are also called Bielids, as they are connected with Biela's comet and move in its orbit.
(Astron.)
A northern constellation, supposed to represent the mythical Andromeda.
(bot.)
A genus of ericaceous flowering plants of northern climates, of which the original species was found growing on a rock surrounded by water.

The apartment appropriated for the males. This was in the lower part of the house.
Produced by the conversion of the stamens into petals, as double flowers, like the garden ranunculus. Brande.
Cannibals; man-eaters; anthropophagi. [R.]
Anthropophagous.
(Bot.)
A support or column on which stamens are raised. Gray.
(Zoöl.)
The part which in some Siphonophora bears the male gonophores.

A very large and important genus of grasses, found in nearly all parts of the world. It includes the lemon grass of Ceylon and the beard grass, or broom sedge, of the United States. The principal subgenus is Sorghum, including A. sorghum and A. halepensis, from which have been derived the Chinese sugar cane, the Johnson grass, the Aleppo grass, the broom corn, and the durra, or Indian millet. Several East Indian species, as A. nardus and A. schonanthus, yield fragrant oils, used in perfumery.
A man sphinx; a sphinx having the head of a man and the body of a lion.
A spore of some algæ, which has male functions.
Having the filaments of the stamens divided into two parts.
Dissection of the human body, as distinguished from zoötomy; anthropotomy. [R.]
A terminal combining form: Having a stamen or stamens; staminate; as, monandrous, with one stamen; polyandrous, with many stamens.
